summary: We developed a platform to mitigate agronomic risks and enhance decision-making accuracy by leveraging real NASA satellite data integrated into the project. The platform analyzes historical data spanning multiple years, including temperature, humidity, soil temperature, and climate conditions, then delivers tailored recommendations based on the producer's specific goals—whether maximizing income or preserving soil health. This project is significant because it boosts producer productivity, reduces crop failure risks, and positively impacts the economy.
details:
What does it do and how does it work?

Stella Root helps soybean farmers in southern Brazil answer one practical question: what should the field do this winter? Wheat to sell, a cover crop for the soil, or a mix of both. The farmer starts on a 3D globe, searches the municipality and lands on Cruz Alta, Rio Grande do Sul. A short form asks about the last seasons: summer and winter crops, how the season went, the main problem and whether the soil is compacted. The app returns a climate report for that place:

  • a month-by-month risk calendar ("in how many of every 10 years did each problem happen") built from 44 years of NASA POWER data;
  • analog years, past seasons whose climate pattern looks like the current one;
  • rotation strategies with regional cover-crop mixes (black oat + vetch, oat + vetch + radish, rye + radish) that balance straw, nitrogen and soil structure.

An interactive map overlays NASA and partner layers for the municipality: SRTM relief, MODIS land surface temperature, GPM IMERG rainfall, SMAP soil moisture, ECOSTRESS, Sentinel-2 NDVI and MapBiomas land use. An AI agronomist chat answers follow-up questions with the same data.

Behind the app, the team published open, reproducible analyses (https://github.com/FieldShift-SpaceApp/fieldshift):

  • Forty years of Landsat show that cropland with probable bare soil in early November fell from 5.7% (1984–94 median) to 0.3% today: it is straw, not bare soil.
  • NASA HLS maps every field's winter since 2020: fallow covers at most 0.6% of the cropland.
  • A free, satellite-side pre-check of Brazil's new soil-management rule for crop insurance (ZarcNM), which recommends Landsat, Sentinel-2 or HLS. In Cruz Alta, 1,263 of 1,286 assessed farms (98%) could reach NM3 or above if the soil test and contour sowing agree.

What benefits does it offer?

  • The data that already exist reach the farmer as an answer to a real decision, not as a dashboard.
  • The decision is made before winter, when it can still change.
  • Every number can be traced to an open source, and the team also publishes what did not hold: winter cover did not protect soybean in the 2021/22 and 2022/23 droughts, and NASA's Prithvi model did not beat simple rules without local labels.

What is the intended impact?

Better winter choices for soybean farms in Rio Grande do Sul, starting with Cruz Alta: more soil protected by straw in the October–November storms, and fewer farms losing the higher insurance subsidy (from 20% up to 40% of the premium in the 2026 pilot) only because nobody checked their management in time. For cooperatives and local governments, the same data show where a soil-test voucher reaches the most small farms.

What tools, programming languages, hardware or software did you use?

  • App: TypeScript, Next.js 16, React 19, Tailwind CSS 4, three.js with React Three Fiber (globe), Leaflet (map), Supabase (prepared data and chat history), the Anthropic Claude API (AI agronomist), deployed on Vercel.
  • Data pipeline: Python scripts for NASA POWER, GPM IMERG, SMAP, GRACE-FO, ECOSTRESS and MODIS (through Google Earth Engine), Sentinel-2, SRTM, MapBiomas, ISRIC SoilGrids, IBGE SIDRA and INMET weather stations.
  • Team analyses: Python 3.12 with NumPy, xarray and pytest; HLS, Landsat and NASADEM read from the Microsoft Planetary Computer.
  • Hardware: the team's own laptops; no special hardware.

What is the creative aspect of your project?

  • It starts from the farmer's own history, not from a map of indices.
  • It travels from planet scale down to one municipality.
  • It turns a new, technical insurance rule into a free preview the farmer can use before deciding. Not a new rating: a free preview of the official one, early enough to change the winter.

What factors did your team consider?

  • The real decision: our agronomist teammate decides the winter in the middle of the soybean season, together with the cooperative's agronomist.
  • Satellite versus ground: NASA POWER is modeled and smooths rain, so the team checks it against INMET stations and ANA rain gauges.
  • Openness and privacy: open data and open code; no personal or property data is published.
  • Who it is for: small farms and cooperatives.
  • What a satellite cannot see: the soil test and contour sowing. That is why the result is always a pre-check, never an official classification.

PROJECT REPOSITORY: https://github.com/FieldShift-SpaceApp/fieldshift

HOW TO TEST: To test the solution, select the municipality of Cruz Alta - RS, in the state of Rio Grande do Sul. We chose this specific region because it has been suffering heavily from climate-related problems in agriculture in Brazil.
dataRefs: SMAP (Soil Moisture Active Passive) - soil moisture
NASA POWER - historical climate series (44 years)
